strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine gap in RAG context compression—the absence of a supervisory signal defining an 'optimal' summary for the downstream LLM—and proposes a sensible solution using downstream task performance (EM/F1) as reward with GRPO.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four QA benchmarks (single-hop and multi-hop), multiple retrievers, consistent backbone for all trainable baselines (RECOMP, NoiseFilter-IB), and comparisons against both small off-the-shelf and very large (DeepSeek-V3) compressors, which makes the headline result—that a 1.5B RL-trained compressor beats both—fair and convincing.

Useful robustness analyses: ablations showing both distillation warm-up and GRPO are necessary (Table 3), compressor-architecture sweeps (Qwen/Llama at 1B/1.5B/3B, Tables 6–7), zero-shot transfer to a different downstream LLM (Table 2), and hyperparameter sensitivity for the F1 reward weight α (Figure 4).

The method does not depend on fixed compression labels and treats the downstream LLM as a black box, which makes it practically applicable; the case studies (Tables 4–5) concretely illustrate why end-to-end optimization helps (e.g., avoiding the misleading 'December 1972' summary).
Implementation details (frameworks, GPUs, hyperparameters, prompts in the appendix) are reported at a level that supports reproduction.
weaknesses: The central 'lossless compression' claim is imprecise and inconsistently stated. The abstract claims a 3% compression ratio, while Section 3.2 says approximately 6%; the per-dataset numbers in Tables 1–2 differ further. Also, compression is not truly 'lossless'—it is a fixed 2-sentence summary that happens to preserve or improve task metrics on the tested datasets. The terminology overstates the guarantee.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting. Improvements of 0.7–3 EM points (e.g., HotpotQA) with single runs and no confidence intervals or seeds make some claims of superiority hard to assess, particularly against DeepSeek-V3 compression where gaps are small.

Efficiency accounting is incomplete. The paper motivates compression by computational cost, but never reports the added latency/overhead of running the compressor at inference time, or the substantial RL training cost (eight H20 GPUs with a 14B reward LLM served via vLLM). The net efficiency benefit is therefore not quantified.

Reward-overfitting / reward-hacking risk is not discussed. The compressor is optimized against the quirks of one evaluator LLM (Qwen2.5-14B) and gold answers; RL could plausibly learn to produce summaries containing hallucinated statements that happen to elicit correct answers (the paper itself observes RECOMP hallucinating). There is no analysis of summary factuality or faithfulness beyond two cherry-picked case studies, and no discussion of failure modes.

Scope and fairness caveats: evaluation is limited to English open-domain QA with a fixed 2-sentence compression budget imposed via the prompt, so 'compression ratio' is largely an artifact of the prompt rather than a learned, controllable quantity; several related compressors discussed in related work (QGC, PISCO, KSE/BIDER) are cited but not compared empirically.

Presentation issues: Figures 1, 3, and 4 are hard to read (overlapping legend, garbled x-axis ticks in Figure 4, '0 0 0.2 0.5 0.5 0.5 1.0'); Tables 6–7 inconsistently use fractions while Table 1 uses percentages; there is no explicit limitations section; and code is only promised ('will be released soon'), which weakens reproducibility at submission time.

strengths: The central idea is sensible and well-motivated: using downstream task accuracy as an RL reward to align the compressor with the needs of the answer-generating LLM directly addresses a real weakness of prior distillation-based compressors such as RECOMP.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four QA benchmarks (single-hop and multi-hop), multiple retrievers, several compression baselines (BM25, off-the-shelf LLMs, DeepSeek-V3, RECOMP, NoiseFilter-IB), a transferability study to a different downstream LLM (Llama-3.1-8B), compressor-architecture robustness (Qwen/Llama 1B/1.5B/3B), an ablation of distillation vs. GRPO, an alpha-sensitivity study, and qualitative case studies.

Reported gains are substantial in places, e.g., +6.9 EM on 2WikiMultihopQA over the full-document baseline at ~3% token budget, and CORE outperforms a 671B-parameter zero-shot compressor, which supports the value of end-to-end optimization.

Implementation details (training framework, GPUs, learning rate, rollouts, KL coefficient, prompts in the appendix) are specified at a level that supports reproduction, and implementation choices are generally clearly described.
weaknesses: The term 'lossless compression' is misleading and used inconsistently. Summarizing ~712 tokens into ~46 tokens is by construction lossy; the paper uses 'lossless' to mean 'no EM/F1 drop,' which conflates compression with downstream accuracy. The abstract claims a 3% compression ratio while Section 3.2 says 'approximately 6%,' and the introduction's headline '3.3 points average EM improvement' vs. 'no loss' framing is confusing. This terminology should be corrected throughout.

The claim of not depending on 'predefined compression labels' is undermined by the method itself: the distillation warm-start is trained on summaries generated by DeepSeek-V3, i.e., teacher-produced compression labels, and the ablation shows removing distillation substantially degrades performance. The honest description is supervision-light RL refinement on top of distilled supervision, not label-free end-to-end training.

The experimental comparison has fairness and leakage concerns that are not fully discussed. CORE is trained per-dataset with the exact downstream LLM (Qwen2.5-14B) used both for reward computation and final evaluation, and distilled data is filtered by that same LLM's correctness. It is unclear whether RECOMP/NoiseFilter-IB received comparable per-dataset training and whether the reward-time prompt matches the evaluation-time few-shot prompt. The improved transfer to Llama-3.1-8B partially mitigates this, but only one held-out LLM is tested.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported, despite the headline claims resting on differences of a few EM points on some datasets (e.g., +0.7 EM on HotpotQA).

Novelty is modest: applying GRPO with a task-accuracy reward to train a summarizer is a fairly direct composition of existing components (GRPO, RECOMP-style compressors, reward-based context filtering as in Kim & Thorne 2025). The paper does not clearly delineate its contribution relative to reward-based filtering prior work.

Efficiency claims are incomplete: the paper reports token counts but no end-to-end wall-clock latency or cost measurements that include the compressor's encoding overhead and the extra LLM inference calls required during RL training, so the practical efficiency benefit of a 'smaller compressor than M' is not quantified.

Potential reward hacking of the frozen downstream LLM is acknowledged implicitly (via transfer experiments) but never analyzed directly, e.g., whether RL-driven summaries exploit formatting or prompting quirks of Qwen2.5-14B rather than genuinely preserving evidence.

Reproducibility is weakened: code is only promised ('will be released soon'), the value of alpha used in the main results is not clearly stated (only a sensitivity analysis is given), and there is no limitations section despite several notable limitations (per-dataset training cost, reliance on a 671B teacher for distillation data, QA-only evaluation).

Presentation issues: Figure 4's x-axis labels are corrupted/duplicated ('0 0.2 0.5 0.5 0.5 1.0'), Figure 3's axis annotations are hard to read, and there are recurring typos ('off-the-shell', 'consripted', 'the the trained compressor'), which suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: using downstream task performance (EM/F1 of a frozen black-box LLM) as an RL reward to train a small compressor via GRPO, thereby aligning compression with what actually helps the downstream task rather than with generic summarization quality.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four QA benchmarks (single-hop and multi-hop), multiple retrievers, several compressor backbones (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama3.2-1B/3B), and fair re-training of RECOMP and NoiseFilter-IB with the same backbone.

Useful generalization analyses: zero-shot transfer of the compressor to a different downstream LLM (Table 2), out-of-domain generalization from 5-doc to 10-doc compression without retraining, and ablations of both the distillation warm-up and GRPO stages (Table 3), plus an alpha sweep for the F1 reward weight.
Qualitative case studies (Tables 4-5) concretely illustrate how the learned compressor extracts answer-critical evidence where baselines introduce misleading statements.

The distillation filtering procedure (retaining only summaries that improve downstream performance, empty target when the question alone suffices) is a thoughtful detail that reduces noisy supervision.
Honest use-of-LLMs statement and reasonable implementation details (frameworks, hyperparameters, hardware).
weaknesses: The 'lossless compression' framing is questionable. The compressor is rewarded purely on downstream EM/F1 and constrained only by a fixed prompt ('2-sentence summary'), so there is no learned or explicitly controlled compression objective; the token budget emerges from the prompt rather than the optimization. No ablation addresses length control or behavior when the summary exceeds the budget.

A potential shortcut is not discussed: the case-study summaries effectively contain (near-)answers to the question. RL could exploit the frozen downstream LLM by outputting answer-like content rather than genuine 'compression.' The paper should analyze or at least acknowledge whether the compressor degenerates into question-answering rather than compression, and how this behaves under distribution shift or unanswerable questions.

Missing important baselines: the LLMLingua family (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua) and Selective-Context are standard, widely used prompt-compression methods for exactly this setting, yet they appear neither in the baselines nor meaningfully in related work. This weakens the SOTA claim.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs are reported; several claimed gains are small (e.g., +0.7 EM on HotpotQA at 10 docs), so the 'improves over no compression' claim rests on single-run point estimates.

The compressor is trained and evaluated on the same four datasets (train/test splits), and the distillation filter uses gold-answer correctness; claims of losslessness are therefore in-distribution, but the paper does not test out-of-distribution compression (e.g., compressors trained on one dataset evaluated on another), which would substantiate the generalization narrative.

Efficiency claims are incomplete: training requires 8 GPUs, a 671B teacher (DeepSeek-V3) for distillation, and LLM inference for every rollout, and at inference the compressor must still encode the full documents; no end-to-end latency/cost analysis or comparison of train-time cost versus inference savings is provided. The use of DeepSeek-V3 both as the distillation teacher and as a compared baseline slightly entangles the comparison.

Evaluation is limited to extractive-style QA with EM/F1 rewards; broader 'downstream task' claims (summarization, generation quality, faithfulness of compressed content) are not tested, and F1-style rewards do not obviously transfer to other task types.
Code is promised but not released ('will be released soon'), limiting immediate reproducibility.

Presentation issues: duplicated text between Section 2.2.4 and Appendix B, typos ('off-the-shell', 'consripted'), Figure 4's x-axis labels appear garbled (0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0), and Figure 1/3 are dense and hard to read. No limitations section discussing reward hacking, data contamination via the December 2018 Wikipedia corpus, or RL training instability.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: framing context compression as an RL problem with direct task performance as reward, removing reliance on proxy heuristics, is a sensible and practically useful idea, especially since the downstream LLM is treated as a frozen black box (no access to internal weights).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: four QA benchmarks (single-hop and multi-hop), strong baseline coverage (BM25, off-the-shelf LLMs, DeepSeek-V3, RECOMP variants, NoiseFilter-IB, LongLLMLingua, QGC) with all trainable baselines using the same backbone for fairness, plus ablations of both training stages, hyperparameter study of alpha, robustness to noisy contexts, LongBench evaluation, and case studies.
Strong empirical results: consistent EM/F1 gains over both full-context RAG and all compression baselines at ~3-6% of the original token count, with gains of 1.5-6.9 EM points over uncompressed RAG.

Good generality analysis: zero-shot transfer to an unseen LLM (Llama-3.1-8B), cross-dataset transfer, and robustness across compressor backbones and scales (1B/1.5B/3B) strengthen the claim that the method learns general compression behavior rather than overfitting to a specific input length.

Practical design choices are well justified: lightweight compressor (order of magnitude smaller than the generator), distillation warm-start addressing limited small-model capacity, and composite EM+F1 reward mitigating reward sparsity. Efficiency analysis (Appendix B) and implementation details (Appendix C) support reproducibility, and code availability is stated.
Honest scoping in Section 3.4 about open-ended tasks, with concrete suggestions for alternative rewards, rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core recipe (SFT warm-start + GRPO with a downstream-task reward) is a fairly standard assembly of existing techniques (DeepSeekMath GRPO, RECOMP-style formulation). Reward-based context compression also exists (e.g., Kim & Thorne 2025), so the contribution is primarily an empirical/systems one rather than a conceptual advance.

Evaluation is confined to extractive QA with EM/F1 rewards; the discussion of open-ended tasks (Section 3.4) is entirely speculative. Since the reward directly encodes the QA metrics, the method's applicability beyond this setting is unverified, which narrows the significance of the claim that CORE generalizes 'naturally beyond extractive QA'.

Potential reward-hacking is not analyzed: optimizing a compressor against the downstream model's EM could yield summaries that exploit model biases or leak answer-like phrasing rather than preserving genuine information content. A human evaluation of summary quality or faithfulness would help rule this out; only two case studies are provided.

No variance or statistical significance reporting: results are single-run point estimates across many small EM differences (often 1-3 points); multiple seeds or confidence intervals are needed to fully support the claimed superiority over strong baselines.

Per-dataset training in the main results raises a mild concern about test-distribution specialization; while cross-dataset transfer is shown (Section 4.7), the transfer setting shows noticeable degradation relative to target-dataset training, and the main-table protocol should be stated more explicitly.

Comparison to the most closely related RL-based compression method (TACO-RL) is argued away rather than empirically tested, and the 'lossless compression' phrasing in the related-work comparison is slightly overclaimed given the improvement (not equality) framing.
Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract appears truncated/incomplete, and Figure 1 is dense and hard to read at print size.

strengths: The core idea of using end-task performance (EM/F1 from the frozen downstream LLM) as a direct reward signal via GRPO is well-motivated and cleanly addresses a genuine weakness of heuristic proxy objectives in RAG context compression.
The two-stage training design (knowledge-distillation warm start followed by RL) is sensible, and the ablation in Table 2 convincingly shows both stages contribute.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four QA benchmarks, LongBench multi-doc QA, multiple compressor backbones (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B), transfer to an unseen LLM (Table 3), transfer to an unseen dataset (Table 4), a noisy-context robustness test (Table 6), and qualitative case studies. Strong results are reported consistently across settings.

The method is practical in spirit: the compressor is deliberately kept small relative to the downstream LLM, the LLM is treated as a black box throughout, and textual summaries remain interpretable and transferable, unlike soft-embedding compression.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear problem formulation and an explicit efficiency analysis (Appendix B).
weaknesses: Limited task scope relative to the claims. All quantitative evaluation is on extractive/single-answer QA with EM and F1. The framework's claimed generality to open-ended tasks (Section 3.4) is purely speculative — no summarization, dialogue, or LLM-as-a-judge experiments are actually run, yet the abstract and conclusion imply broad applicability. The central 'performance-driven' premise is only validated for binary/near-binary rewards.

Novelty is overstated. The paper repeatedly claims to 'eliminate reliance on proxy heuristics,' but EM against gold answers is itself a heuristic proxy for true utility, and prior work already applies reward-based optimization to context selection/compression for QA (e.g., Kim & Thorne 2025 cited in the paper, TACO-RL). The contribution is essentially a competent combination of distillation warm start + GRPO with an EM+F1 reward, applied to a known problem setting (RECOMP's formulation is adopted verbatim).

Risk of overfitting to the (LLM, dataset) pair used during RL is acknowledged only implicitly ('intrinsic compression patterns') and never tested rigorously. The cross-LLM and cross-dataset transfers are zero-shot anecdotes on single (source, target) pairs; a systematic study varying the reward-generating LLM during training is missing.

No statistical rigor: results are single runs with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite many reported differences of 1–3 EM points being interpreted as meaningful. Hyperparameters (e.g., alpha) appear tuned on test-adjacent settings — the development/test protocol for HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA is not clearly separated.

The headline '3% compression ratio' and 'lossless' framing are somewhat misleading: the method compresses the top-5/top-10 retrieved short passages (~700–1500 tokens) to ~35–50 tokens; claims of 'true lossless compression' are not substantiated beyond QA accuracy on the tested benchmarks.

Baseline fairness concerns: DeepSeek-V3 (671B) is used zero-shot as a 'baseline compressor,' which is not a trained compression baseline and mainly serves to flatter the comparison; other recent trainable or RL-based compressors are not compared head-to-head.
No dedicated limitations section; the code link in the abstract is empty ('available at' with nothing following), which weakens reproducibility despite detailed implementation notes in Appendix C.
Case studies are cherry-picked single examples; no quantitative error analysis (e.g., how often CORE introduces factual errors or omits answer-critical evidence) is provided.

strengths: The core idea—using downstream task performance (EM + token-F1) as an RL reward via GRPO, with a distillation warm-start from a large teacher (DeepSeek-V3)—is a sensible and well-motivated way to remove the proxy-heuristic bottleneck in RAG context compression, and the framing (compressor as policy, downstream LLM as frozen black box) is clearly articulated.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and mostly convincing: four QA benchmarks spanning single-hop and multi-hop, comparisons against multiple recent trainable baselines (RECOMP, NoiseFilter-IB, LongLLMLingua, QGC) trained on the same backbone for fairness, an out-of-scale DeepSeek-V3 compressor baseline, and ablations isolating both training stages (Table 2).

The generalization studies are a genuine strength: zero-shot transfer to an unseen LLM (Llama-3.1-8B, Table 3), cross-dataset transfer (Table 4), length extrapolation from 5 to 10 retrieved documents, robustness to noisy/adversarial retrievals (Table 6), and extension to long-context settings on LongBench (Table 5).

Multiple compressor backbones and scales (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B) are evaluated, supporting the claim that the framework is model-agnostic and benefits from compressor scale (Figures 5, Tables 7-8).

The paper is well written and organized; the two-phase training pipeline is clearly described, implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, training time) are provided in the appendix, and case studies (Tables 9-10) give qualitative insight into why learned compression beats heuristic baselines.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the method is essentially a careful combination of existing components (SFT warm-start plus GRPO with a task-metric reward). The reward design (EM + token-level F1) and the data curation rules in Section 3.2.1 are reasonable but straightforward; the contribution rests primarily on empirical validation rather than a new technique or analysis.

Evaluation is confined to extractive/factoid QA with EM/F1-style rewards. Section 3.4 on open-ended tasks (summarization, dialogue, long-form generation) is purely speculative—no experiment validates that the framework works with LLM-as-a-judge or metric-based rewards, so the claim that 'CORE should generalize naturally beyond extractive QA' is unsupported.

Potential reward-hacking / shortcut-learning is not analyzed. Because the reward is derived from the downstream LLM's answer, the compressor could learn to leak answer patterns rather than produce faithful summaries; faithfulness/hallucination of the compressed summaries is never quantitatively measured (the case studies are anecdotal).

There is an apparent inconsistency about the compression ratio: Figure 1 advertises a '3 tok' context for CORE-RAG, while Figure 2 and Table 1 show summaries of roughly 32-59 tokens; the abstract's '3% compression ratio' and 'exponentially large DeepSeek model' claims should be stated more carefully.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., multiple seeds for RL training, confidence intervals) despite RL training being inherently high-variance; some reported margins over strong baselines (e.g., QGC) are modest.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract states 'Our code is available at' but the URL is missing in the manuscript. Training also requires black-box reward queries to a 14B LLM served via vLLM during RL, and the total end-to-end inference latency (compressor + LLM) versus full-context RAG is discussed only qualitatively in Appendix B without measured latency numbers.

Some relevant baselines are omitted or only briefly mentioned, e.g., soft/compressive-embedding approaches like xRAG (cited but not compared) and TACO-RL, which the related-work section itself positions as closest in spirit.
